theme: Blessed be the LORD; his glory fills the earth
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 72 in full, giving special attention to the closing doxology in verses 18 and 19. This is a prayer for the king, and it closes the second book of the Psalter. Notice how a prayer for a human king grows into a prayer for the whole earth to be filled with God’s glory.
settingTheScene: Psalm 72 is a psalm “of Solomon,” or perhaps for Solomon, a prayer that the king would rule with God’s justice and bring blessing to the nations. It ends Book II of the Psalter with a doxology (vv. 18-19) and a note: “The prayers of David, the son of Jesse, are ended.” The psalm describes a king far greater than any Israel ever had: one whose reign extends from sea to sea, whose name endures forever, and through whom all nations are blessed. This is the promise to Abraham (Genesis 12:3) and to David (2 Samuel 7), and the New Testament sees its fulfillment in Jesus. In Revelation, kings do bring their glory into the city (21:24), and the whole earth is filled with the glory of the Lord.
observation: “Give the king your justice, O God, and your righteousness to the royal son!” (v. 1).
“May he defend the cause of the poor of the people, give deliverance to the children of the needy, and crush the oppressor!” (v. 4).
“May he have dominion from sea to sea, and from the River to the ends of the earth!” (v. 8).
“May all kings fall down before him, all nations serve him!” (v. 11).
“May people be blessed in him, all nations call him blessed!” (v. 17).
“Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who alone does wondrous things” (v. 18).
“Blessed be his glorious name forever; may the whole earth be filled with his glory! Amen and Amen!” (v. 19).
“The prayers of David, the son of Jesse, are ended” (v. 20).
interpretation:
The psalm begins as a prayer for the king: “Give the king your justice, O God, and your righteousness to the royal son!” The test of a good king is whether he rules with God’s justice. Specifically, “May he defend the cause of the poor of the people, give deliverance to the children of the needy, and crush the oppressor!” The poor are the king’s first concern. Justice for the vulnerable is central to a godly government and to the reign of Christ.

The prayer then pictures a reign of peace and abundance: “May the mountains bear prosperity for the people, and the hills, in righteousness!” The king will be like rain on mown grass, like showers that water the earth. “In his days may the righteous flourish, and peace abound, till the moon be no more!” His rule extends “from sea to sea, and from the River to the ends of the earth.” Foreign kings bring tribute: “May the kings of Tarshish and of the isles render him tribute; may the kings of Sheba and Seba bring gifts! May all kings fall down before him, all nations serve him!” This echoes the gifts of the wise men to the infant Christ and the vision of the nations bringing their glory into the New Jerusalem. The reason is again compassion: “For he delivers the needy when he calls, the poor and him who has no helper. He has pity on the weak and the needy, and saves the lives of the needy.” He redeems their lives from oppression and violence, and “precious is their blood in his sight.”

The prayer reaches its high point in verse 17: “May his name endure forever, his fame continue as long as the sun! May people be blessed in him, all nations call him blessed!” This is an echo of the Abrahamic promise: “in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 12:3). No merely human king could fulfill this. Solomon’s reign had a golden beginning but ended in compromise, and the kings after him fell. The psalm remained a prayer for a king who would fulfill it. Jesus is that King. He defends the poor, saves the needy, and brings blessing to all nations. “Behold, something greater than Solomon is here” (Matthew 12:42).

The psalm ends with a doxology that closes Book II: “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who alone does wondrous things. Blessed be his glorious name forever; may the whole earth be filled with his glory! Amen and Amen!” The prayer for the king becomes a prayer for God’s glory over the whole earth. This is the goal of everything: not the king’s honor but the glory of God. The doxology answers Numbers 14:21 and anticipates Habakkuk 2:14. And then the note, “The prayers of David, the son of Jesse, are ended.” The prayers of a man end, but the prayer for God’s kingdom goes on in the prayer Jesus taught us: “Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.” It will be answered fully in the new creation, when the whole earth is filled with his glory.
connection: 2 Samuel 7:12-16 and Genesis 12:1-3 are the promises behind the psalm. 1 Kings 3-10 shows Solomon’s reign. Matthew 2:1-12 shows kings bringing gifts to Jesus. Matthew 12:42 and Luke 1:32-33 declare Jesus greater than Solomon. Isaiah 11:1-9 and 9:6-7 describe the righteous king. Numbers 14:21 and Habakkuk 2:14 speak of the earth filled with God’s glory. Matthew 6:10 is the prayer for his kingdom to come. Psalm 41:13, 89:52, and 106:48 are the other doxologies closing the books of the Psalter. Revelation 5:9-14, 11:15, and 21:24-26 show the nations and kings worshiping.
application:
Pray Matthew 6:10 slowly: your kingdom come, your will be done. Name one place where you long to see his justice.

Ask how you can “defend the cause of the poor” in a practical way this month through your time, giving, or voice.

End your day with verse 19: “Blessed be his glorious name forever; may the whole earth be filled with his glory! Amen and Amen!”
prayerPrompts: Bless the LORD who alone does wondrous things.
Thank him for the true King, Jesus.
Ask him to fill the earth with his glory.
